BattleTech Miniature Scale for 3D Printing

BattleTech runs at a small 6mm epic scale, which flips the usual advice upside down. The mechs are chunky enough that FDM handles them well, but they are small enough that judging detail at this size takes practice. Getting the mech onto or off the arguably-irrelevant base is where most sizing conversations start.

What scale am I actually printing?

Miniature Scale
6mm
Ratio Equivalent
1:285
Measurement
top of machine
Eye Level Height
5.7mm

BattleTech 'mechs represent machines 9-15 meters tall. At 1:285 scale, a 12-meter 'mech should be about 42mm tall, but actual miniatures vary widely — Catalyst's modern sculpts are closer to 1:265 (slightly larger than true 1:285). Older Iron Wind Metals miniatures are smaller and closer to the original ratio. Scale consistency within the range matters more than mathematical accuracy.

Publisher: Catalyst Game Labs·Base Sizes: Hex-based (no traditional bases)

At 6mm, my advice is to think about the mech's silhouette rather than fine texture. The analog scale matters, but what reads on the table is the overall shape and stance. FDM at 6mm rewards building the profile correctly with a fine nozzle and a steady hand.

I cluster small mechs onto a single build plate and print several in one go, which makes the per-mech time essentially irrelevant. Because they are small, support scarring is proportionally more damaging, so I favour orientations that minimize overhangs on arms and legs.

Deep Dive: 6mm 'mechs — from 30 to 55mm tall

BattleTech is 6mm (about 1:285), but a 'mech's height depends on its weight class, so Light 'mechs run 30mm tall and Assaults run 55mm. Printing proxies is about matching Catalyst's modern sculpts, not a strict ratio.

Why '6mm' Is a Moving Target

BattleTech 'mechs represent machines 9-15 meters tall. At 1:285 scale a 12-meter 'mech should be about 42mm tall, but the actual range varies a lot. Catalyst's modern sculpts run closer to 1:265 (slightly larger than true ratio), while older Iron Wind Metals miniatures are smaller and closer to the original math. The scale is a family, not a single number.

Match the Range, Not the Math

The reliable approach is to pick one official miniature as your reference and match its height. I keep a single Catalyst 'mech on the bench and measure every printed proxy against it. Consistency within a lance matters more than hitting a strict 1:285 ratio — the game is hex-based and scale-perfect models are the least of your worries.

FDM Limits at This Size

'Mechs are small but dense with detail — cockpit glass, weapon barrels, and antennas all need to read. I print the machines at 0.2mm nozzle and 0.04-0.06mm layers, and print terrain and hex tiles with a 0.4mm nozzle. Magnetizing bases makes transport easier, since small models shift around in a case.

These are the validated reference steps I use when a printed model spans the small-scale ranges. They rarely apply to 'mechs directly — your reference miniature is the better guide.

Common BattleTech Mistakes

  • Scaling a Light and an Assault to the same height. Weight class differences are real and add to the game's readability.
  • Scaling to strict 1:285 math. You will undersize modern Catalyst sculpts — match the range instead.
  • FDM on cockpits and antennas. At 6mm those details need a 0.2mm nozzle, or they come out as blobs.

Printing these minis on FDM

6mm mechs are small but chunky, so a 0.2mm nozzle with fine layers keeps the profile clean. Print several at once on one plate for efficiency and prefer upright orientations to reduce supports.

All settings tested on my Bambu Lab A1 Mini with PLA. Your printer may want something different — always print a test piece first.

Frequently Asked Questions

What scale is BattleTech?
BattleTech is 6mm epic scale focused on vehicles and mechs rather than individual infantry.
Can an FDM printer handle 6mm mechs?
Yes, mechs are chunky enough to read well. Use a 0.2mm nozzle and print several at once on one plate.
